name: Kava (kavalactones)

lead: Kava is a traditional Pacific root drink, now also sold as capsules and extracts, used for relaxation and stress. Users take it to ease anxiety and sleep better, on the idea that lower tension shows as a more relaxed, rested face.

Kavalactones are thought to act on GABA-A, dopamine and other receptors, though the mechanism is not well established. A 2003 systematic review reported a small anxiety benefit over placebo, while some health bodies conclude the evidence does not support effectiveness for generalized anxiety disorder. Appearance has not been studied.

paras: It is taken as a traditional drink or as capsules and extracts, often in the evening for winding down. Users describe the effect as relaxation that can build into easier sleep.

Reports of rare severe liver injury in the early 2000s led to bans or restrictions in several countries, some since revised; regulators and the WHO distinguish water-based traditional kava from solvent extracts. It interacts with alcohol and some drugs, and legal status varies by country.

angle.text: Users take kava to unwind, ease anxiety and sleep better, so lower stress shows in a more relaxed, rested face. Small trials have looked at anxiety.

lead: Kava is a drink and extract made from the roots of Piper methysticum, a plant domesticated in the Pacific Islands, where it is used socially and ceremonially. Its main active constituents are kavalactones, of which six account for most of its pharmacological activity.[1][2] In supplement form, it is used for anxiety, stress and sleep.

In vitro work indicates kavalactones act on GABA-A, dopamine and other receptors, though the precise mechanism is not fully understood.[1] A 2003 systematic review reported a small anxiety benefit over placebo, while some health bodies conclude the evidence does not support effectiveness for generalized anxiety disorder.[1]

Kava drew regulatory attention in the early 2000s after reports of liver injury linked to extracts, leading to bans or restrictions in several countries; several have since been revised.[1] It has no studied appearance use and appears as a recovery-category herb.
infobox: Kavain, dihydrokavain, methysticin, dihydromethysticin, yangonin, desmethoxyyangonin
Traditional water drink; capsule and extract supplements
Varies; US dietary supplement; UK medicinal sale offence

paras: Traditionally kava is prepared as a water infusion and drunk socially in Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia, central to ceremonies such as the sevusevu in Fiji and the nakamal in Vanuatu.[1][2] In Western markets it is sold as capsules, extracts and drinks for relaxation, and kava bars operate in several US cities.[1]

Laboratory studies indicate modulation of GABA-A, dopamine, norepinephrine and cannabinoid CB1 receptors and inhibition of MAO-B and ion channels, but the page-level consensus is that molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood.[1][3]

Heavy long-term use is associated with a reversible dry, scaly skin condition called kava dermopathy. Kava can interact with alcohol, benzodiazepines and levodopa, and caution is advised in pregnancy and liver disease.[1][4]

In 2002 the FDA warned of rare but severe liver injury from kava supplements. The WHO judged moderate consumption of traditional water-based kava to carry an acceptably low risk, and linked liver injury to ethanolic and acetonic extracts. A 2017 European committee found the benefit-risk balance for oral kava in anxiety unfavorable.[1] Grokipedia attributes much of the toxicity to extract quality and contaminants, a position that has been debated.[2]

Following 2002 liver-safety concerns, the EU, Singapore and Canada restricted kava; Canada lifted its restrictions in 2012. A German court overturned that country's ban in 2014. Selling medicinal kava in the United Kingdom is a criminal offence, though personal possession is legal. In the US it is sold as a dietary supplement and the FDA concluded in 2020 that it is not generally recognized as safe for conventional foods. Australia's TGA recommends a daily cap on kavalactone intake.[1]
No community discussion of kava was available for this entry; any interest relates to its use for stress and sleep rather than appearance.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of kava extract for anxiety reported a small benefit over placebo, in some analyses comparable to oxazepam and buspirone, with the strongest data from multiweek trials of aqueous extracts; results were mixed and standardized trials are limited.[1] Public health bodies cited on the reference page conclude current evidence does not support effectiveness for generalized anxiety disorder.[1]

Registered studies have examined kava pharmacokinetics, anxiety and stress in cancer survivors (withdrawn), a phase 2 anxiolytic study, interactions with nicotine metabolism, and combinations with kratom.[5][6][7][8] No studies of kava for appearance were found.

timeline.event: Kava domesticated in northern Vanuatu, per reference accounts.[1]
European naturalists document the drink during Cook's Pacific voyages.[2]
Liver-safety concerns prompt bans and warnings in several countries, including an FDA consumer advisory.[1]
A German court overturns the national kava ban.[1]
